results.title: Instances of undirected Hamiltonian path
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of undirected Hamiltonian path is a pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a finite list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edge list.

results.title: Graph of an undirected Hamiltonian path instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an instance $(n, E)$ of undirected Hamiltonian path, its graph is the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

results.title: Well-formed undirected Hamiltonian path instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E)$ of undirected Hamiltonian path is well formed when $n > 0$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and the reversed pair $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

results.title: Feasible undirected Hamiltonian path instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E)$ of undirected Hamiltonian path is feasible when its graph has a Hamiltonian path: a list of length $n$ of vertices of the graph, with no repeated entries and containing every vertex, in which any two consecutive entries are adjacent.

results.title: HAMILTONIAN PATH (UNDIRECTED) as a decision problem

results.title: HAMILTONIAN PATH (UNDIRECTED) is NP-complete

The result is $(s, t, n, E)$, with $E$ the list of these pairs in order; there is no result unless the input ends right after $n$ or…

results.title: Arcs of the PATH digraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, there is an arc from $u$ to $v$ when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$; listed pairs with an end at least $n$ give no arc.

results.title: The PATH problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: PATH is the decision problem that accepts a bit string $x$ exactly when $x$ is the encoding of some instance $(s, t, n, E)$ with $s < n$, $t < n$ and a sequence $s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$ with $k \ge 0$ such that each $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an arc, that is, a pair listed in $E$ with both ends below $n$.

results.title: Initial marks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$, the initial marks are the list of $n$ booleans whose entry at position $i < n$ is true exactly when $i = s$; all entries are false when $s \ge n$.

results.title: One marking pass
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an edge list $E$ and a list $m$ of booleans (the marks), the pass scans the pairs $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order and, whenever $u < n$, $v < n$ and position $u$ of the current marks is true, sets position $v$ to true. A position beyond the end of the list counts as false and setting it changes nothing. Marks set earlier in the pass are seen by later pairs.

results.title: Reach marks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and an edge list $E$, the reach marks are obtained from the initial marks of $s$ among $0, \dots, n - 1$ by applying the marking pass over $E$ with bound $n$ exactly $n$ times.

results.title: The marking algorithm for PATH
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: On a bit string $x$, the check decodes $x$ as a PATH instance. If decoding fails it returns false; if it yields $(s, t, n, E)$ it returns true exactly when $s < n$, $t < n$ and position $t$ of the marks after $n$ marking passes from $s$ over $E$ is true.

results.title: Decoding inverts the PATH instance encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$ succeeds and returns $(s, t, n, E)$.

results.title: The PATH instance parser succeeds exactly on encodings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a bit string $x$, natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to $x$ succeeds with result $(s, t, n, E)$ if and only if $x$ is the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$.

results.title: The PATH instance encoding is injective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s, t, n, s', t', n'$ be natural numbers and $E, E'$ lists of pairs of natural numbers. If the PATH instance encodings of $(s, t, n, E)$ and $(s', t', n', E')$ are equal, then $s = s'$, $t = t'$, $n = n'$ and $E = E'$.

results.title: Setting an entry of a boolean list to true
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a list of booleans and $v, w$ natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Set the entry of $m$ at position $w$ to $\mathrm{true}$, leaving $m$ unchanged if $w$ is not less than the length of $m$. Then position $v$ of the result holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if position $v$ of $m$ holds $\mathrm{true}$, or $v = w$ and $w$ is less than the length of $m$.

results.title: The initial marks mark exactly the source, if it is a vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n, s, v$ be natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Position $v$ of the initial marks for $n$ vertices and source $s$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if $v < n$ and $v = s$.

results.title: A marking pass preserves the length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. A marking pass over $E$ for $n$ vertices, applied to $m$, gives a list of the same length as $m$.

results.title: Marks persist through a pass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n, v \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans. If $v < |m|$ and the $v$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true, then the same holds for the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.

results.title: Soundness of a pass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $P$ be a property of natural numbers and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers such that $P(u)$ implies $P(v)$ whenever $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$. If $m$ is a list of booleans such that $P(v)$ holds for every $v < |m|$ whose entry in $m$ is true, then $P(v)$ holds for every $v$ whose entry is true in the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.

results.title: A pass marks the heads of arcs with marked tails
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans, where $m$ marks $w$ when $w < |m|$ and the $w$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true. If $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v < |m|$ and $m$ marks $u$, then the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$ marks $v$.

results.title: Counting true entries of pointwise dominated boolean lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists of booleans of the same length such that every position holding $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_1$ also holds $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_2$. Then $l_1$ has at most as many $\mathrm{true}$ entries as $l_2$, and strictly fewer if $l_1 \ne l_2$.

results.title: A pass either changes nothing or adds a mark
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and every list $m$ of booleans, let $m'$ be the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$. Then $m' = m$, or $m'$ has strictly more entries equal to true than $m$.

results.title: Repeated marking passes preserve the length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. For every natural number $k$, applying $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices to $m$ gives a list of the same length as $m$.

results.title: Marks survive repeated passes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ and $v$ be natural numbers, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans whose position $v$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ (positions at or beyond the end read as $\mathrm{false}$). Then for every natural number $k$, position $v$ still holds $\mathrm{true}$ after $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from $m$.

results.title: The final marks have one entry per vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n, s$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the marks after $n$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from the initial marks for source $s$, form a list of length $n$.

results.title: Repeated passes reach a fixpoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Let $r$ be the list obtained from the initial marks (only $s$ marked among $0, \dots, n - 1$) by $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then one more marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ leaves $r$ unchanged.

results.title: The final marks are exactly the reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n, s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and $t < n$, and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Start from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ in which only $s$ is marked and apply $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then $t$ is marked if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs of $E$ below $n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$.

results.title: The marking algorithm decides PATH
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit string $x$, the marking algorithm returns the same answer on $x$ as the decision problem PATH.

results.title: Stack alphabets of the PATH marking machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The output stack $O$ of the PATH marking machine holds Booleans, and every other stack holds symbols of the SAT verifier's symbol alphabet.

results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The statements of the multi-stack Turing machine (TM2) model whose stacks carry the stack alphabets $\Gamma$ of the marking machine, whose labels are the labels of the marking machine, and whose internal state is a boolean.

results.title: The counter unit of the PATH marking machine
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The unit symbol of the counters of the PATH marking machine is the clause-end symbol $\mathrm{cl}$ of the SAT verifier's symbol alphabet.

results.title: Walk step of the PATH marking machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a counter stack $c$, a label $\ell$ and a final statement $f$, the walk step pops the top of $c$. If $c$ was nonempty, it goes to $\ell$ after moving the top mark of the marks stack $M$, if there is one, onto the parked stack $P$: the mark is popped, read as a bit (a symbol that is not a bit reads as false), and pushed on $P$ as that bit. If $c$ was empty, it runs $f$.

results.title: Mark-setting step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a label $\ell$, the statement of the marking machine that pops the top cell of the mark stack $M$ and, if there was one, pushes the set mark (the bit true) onto $M$ in its place; in either case it then goes to $\ell$.

results.title: The marking machine for PATH
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The multi-stack machine program whose input lies on the stack $X$ and whose answer is pushed on the Boolean stack $O$. To read a unary number off $X$ onto a stack $d$, it pops a bit off $X$ and pushes it on $d$, repeating while the bit is true and moving on after the first false bit; an empty $X$ jumps to `bad`. results.title: Start label of the PATH marking machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The marking machine for PATH starts at the label that reads the source vertex $s$, in unary, off the input.

results.title: Setting the first mark
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of booleans, the list obtained by setting its first entry: the empty list is left unchanged, and a list $b :: r$ with first entry $b$ and remaining entries $r$ becomes $\mathrm{true} :: r$.

results.title: Setting an entry by splitting the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $m$ of booleans and every natural number $j$, the first $j$ entries of $m$ followed by the remaining entries with their first entry set to true (the empty list stays empty) equal $m$ with entry $j$ set to true (which is $m$ itself when $j \ge |m|$).

results.title: Reading the mark of vertex $j$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a list of Boolean marks and $j$ a natural number. Drop the first $j$ marks of $m$ and write the rest as bit symbols; reading the top symbol as a bit, with false when there is no top symbol, gives the entry of $m$ at position $j$ (counting from $0$), or false when $j$ is at least the length of $m$.

results.title: Out-of-range arcs need no guard
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a list of $n$ Boolean marks and let $u$, $v$ be natural numbers; write $m_u$ for the entry of $m$ at position $u$ (counting from $0$), taken to be false when $u \ge n$. If $u < n$, $v < n$ and $m_u$ is true, set position $v$ of $m$ to true, and otherwise keep $m$; the result is the same as setting position $v$ of $m$ to true when $m_u$ is true and keeping $m$ otherwise.

results.title: Initial marks by setting one entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $s$, setting entry $s$ of the list of $n$ copies of false to true (which changes nothing when $s \ge n$) gives the initial marks of $n$ vertices from $s$: the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is true exactly when $i = s$.

results.title: A cleared mark or nothing reads as cleared
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every decidable proposition $p$, the optional mark that is a cleared mark (false) when $p$ holds and absent otherwise, read with default false, is false.

results.title: A pass sets no mark when none is set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and every list $es$ of arcs of natural numbers, one pass of the marking algorithm with $n$ vertices over $es$ (Mark Pass) maps the list of $k$ cleared marks to itself.

results.title: The marking algorithm reads the mark of the target
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a bit string $x$ parses as a PATH instance with source $s$, target $t$, $n$ vertices and edge list $es$, then the marking algorithm on $x$ returns the mark of $t$ in the reach marks of $s$ (the marks after $n$ marking passes over $es$, starting from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ with only $s$ marked, and none if $s \ge n$), where a vertex $t \ge n$ counts as unmarked.

results.title: Agreement off a set of stacks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and two contents $S$, $S'$ of its stacks, $S'$ agrees with $S$ off $A$ when every stack not in $A$ holds the same list in $S'$ as in $S$.

results.title: Frames are reflexive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and every assignment $S$ of contents to its stacks, $S$ agrees with itself off $A$.

results.title: Frames compose
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be lists of stacks such that every stack in $A$ or in $B$ is in $C$. If stacks $S_2$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $A$, and $S_3$ agree with $S_2$ on every stack outside $B$, then $S_3$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $C$.

results.title: Updating a framed stack preserves the frame
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a list of stacks of the PATH marking machine, and let $S$ and $S'$ be stack contents such that $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every stack outside $A$. Then for every stack $k \in A$ and every list $l$ over the alphabet of $k$, the contents obtained from $S'$ by replacing stack $k$ with $l$ still agree with $S$ on every stack outside $A$.

results.summary: Let $c$ be a stack, $\mathit{self}$ a label, $\mathit{fin}$ a statement and $S$ stacks in which $c$ is empty. For every internal state $v$, executing from $v$ and $S$ the walk step counted by $c$ that loops at $\mathit{self}$ and finishes with $\mathit{fin}$ gives the same result as executing $\mathit{fin}$ from internal state false and the same stacks $S$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\ell$ be a label, $v$ an internal state and $S$ stacks whose mark stack $M$ holds the bits of a list $l$ of booleans. Executing the mark-setting step to $\ell$ from internal state $v$ and stacks $S$ ends at label $\ell$ with some internal state and the stacks $S$ with $M$ replaced by the bits of $l$ with its first entry set to true (the empty list stays empty); every other stack is unchanged.

results.title: The marking algorithm is polynomial-time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The marking algorithm for PATH, as a function from bit strings to booleans, is computable in polynomial time by a Turing machine with respect to the canonical bitstring encodings of lists of booleans and of booleans.

results.title: Fenwick tree
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ is an array of elements of $\alpha$, read as one-indexed interval sums with an unused dummy entry at index $0$. The structure itself imposes no condition on the entries, and the underlying array it represents is not stored; the relation saying that a tree represents a given array is defined separately.

results.title: Lowest set bit
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the largest power of two dividing $n$; for $n = 0$ it is defined as $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.

results.title: Lowbit of zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: By convention, $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.

results.title: The lowest set bit of a positive number is positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) > 0$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.

results.title: The lowest set bit is at most the number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) \le n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$).

results.title: The lowest set bit divides the number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ divides $n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.

results.title: The lowest set bit is a power of two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is a power of two: $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.

results.title: Dividing out the lowest set bit leaves an odd number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, the quotient $n / \operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is odd, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.

results.title: Fenwick-tree interval sum of a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $a$ of elements of a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, the interval sum at the one-indexed position $j$ is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$ (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the end of $a$ count as $0$.

results.title: Interval sum read from an array
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an array $a$ of elements of a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, this is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$ (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the end of $a$ count as $0$.

results.title: Fenwick tree representing a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid represents a list $a$ of length $n$ when its stored array has length $n + 1$ (a dummy entry at index $0$ plus one entry per element of $a$) and, for every $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$, the stored entry at index $j$ equals the block sum of $a$ at $j$: the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at position $j - 1$ (positions counted from $0$),…

results.title: Size of a Fenwick tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a Fenwick tree is the length of its stored array minus one, truncated at $0$; the one accounts for the dummy entry at index $0$. It is read off the stored array in constant time.

results.title: A Fenwick tree has the length of the list it represents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid represents a list $a$, then the size of $t$ equals the length of $a$.

results.title: Building a Fenwick tree from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ stores the array of length $n + 1$ whose entry at index $0$ is $0$ and whose entry at each one-indexed position $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$ is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$.

results.title: Size of a built Fenwick tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $a$ over an additive commutative monoid, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ has size equal to the length of $a$.

results.title: Building a Fenwick tree yields a valid representation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $a$ over an additive commutative monoid, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ represents $a$.

results.title: Fenwick tree prefix sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over an additive commutative monoid with $n$ underlying entries, let $k$ be a natural number and let $m = \min(k, n)$. The prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ is the sum of the stored entries of $t$ at the positions $j_0 = m$, $j_{r+1} = j_r - \operatorname{lowbit}(j_r)$, taken for as long as $j_r > 0$.

results.title: The empty prefix sum is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid, the prefix sum of length $0$ of $t$ is $0$.

results.title: Correctness of Fenwick tree prefix sums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a$ of elements of an additive commutative monoid. Then for every natural number $k$, including $k > |a|$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries of $a$.

results.title: Prefix sums of a built Fenwick tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $a$ of elements of an additive commutative monoid and every natural number $k$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of the Fenwick tree built from $a$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries of $a$.

results.title: Out-of-range point updates leave a Fenwick tree unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, and let $n$ be its size (the length of its stored array minus one). For every natural number $i \ge n$ and every $\delta \in \alpha$, the point update of $t$ adding $\delta$ at position $i$ returns $t$ itself.

results.title: Point update preserves representation
results.caption: Theorem

For every index $i < n$ (counting from $0$) and every element $\delta$, the tree obtained from $t$ by adding $\delta$ at position $i$ represents the list obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry $a_i$ with $a_i + \delta$.

results.title: Fenwick tree range sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative group and natural numbers $\mathit{lo}$ and $\mathit{hi}$, the range sum of $t$ over $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ is $0$ if $\mathit{hi} \le \mathit{lo}$, and otherwise the prefix sum of length $\mathit{hi}$ of $t$ minus the prefix sum of length $\mathit{lo}$ of $t$.

results.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of elements of an additive commutative group. results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The aggregate of a segment tree with values in an additive monoid is $0$ for the empty tree, $x$ for a single leaf with value $x$, and the aggregate cached at the root for an internal node.

results.title: Size of a segment tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a segment tree is $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and, for an internal node, the segment length cached at that node.

results.caption: Definition

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every internal node of a segment tree, with any cached aggregate, any cached length, left child $L$ and right child $R$, its leaf list is the leaf list of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.

results.summary: For every list $xs$ over an additive monoid, the segment tree built from $xs$ is valid.

results.title: Point update preserves the size of a segment tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every segment tree $t$ over an additive monoid, every index $i$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ has the same size as $t$.

results.title: Point update preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Deterministic ski-rental strategy
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A deterministic strategy is either a day $t \in \mathbb{N}$ on which to buy the skis, after renting on the days before it, or the choice to rent forever. Days are numbered from $1$; the value $t = 0$ is also a strategy, and the cost treats it as renting forever.

results.title: Cost of a ski-rental strategy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Renting skis costs $1$ per day and buying them costs a natural number $B$. The cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d) \in \mathbb{N}$ of a strategy $s$ for a season of $d \in \mathbb{N}$ days is $(t - 1) + B$ if $s$ buys on a day $t$ with $1 \le t \le d$ (rent for $t - 1$ days, then buy), and $d$ otherwise, that is, if $s$ rents forever or buys on a day $t$ with $t = 0$ or $t > d$ (rent every day).

results.title: Offline optimum for ski rental
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a purchase price $B \in \mathbb{N}$ and a season of $d \in \mathbb{N}$ days, the offline optimum is $\mathrm{opt}_B(d) = \min(d, B)$: rent every day or buy on day one, whichever is cheaper.

results.title: Break-even strategy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a purchase price $B$, the break-even strategy is the deterministic strategy that buys on day $B$.

results.title: The offline optimum bounds every strategy's cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every purchase price $B$, every deterministic strategy $s$ and every season length $d$, the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$ is at most the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d)$ of $s$ for a season of $d$ days.

results.title: Ski-rental upper bound for the break-even strategy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every purchase price $B \ge 1$ and every season length $d$, the break-even strategy $\mathrm{breakEven}_B$ pays at most $2 - 1/B$ times the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$: its cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$ for a season of $d$ days satisfies $B \cdot \mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d) \le (2B - 1) \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$.

results.title: The break-even strategy pays at most twice the optimum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every purchase price $B \ge 1$ and every season length $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$ of the break-even strategy for a season of $d$ days is at most $2 \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$, twice the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$. In particular, the break-even strategy is $2$-competitive.

results.title: Lower bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every deterministic strategy pays at least `(2 - 1/B)` times the optimum on some season, `(2 B - 1) * opt ≤ B * cost`.
